h1: Red wine maceration: getting colour and tannin out of the skins
title: Red Wine Maceration and Extraction | Craft Beer School
desc: How red winemakers extract colour and tannin from grape skins: cold soak, cap management, fermentation temperature and pressing.
teaser: Every red wine's colour and tannin come from the skins. How you work the cap decides how much you get.
standfirst: Red wine gets its colour, tannin and much of its flavour from the grape skins. Maceration is how winemakers control that extraction. This guide covers the methods, the numbers and the risks for a small winery.
sections:
The juice of almost all red grapes is clear. Colour lives in the skins as anthocyanin pigments. Tannins live in skins and seeds. Many aroma compounds sit in or just under the skin too. Maceration means keeping the juice and then the wine in contact with skins so these compounds move into it.

How long, how warm and how actively you work the skins decides the style: a light, fruity red or a deep, structured one built to age. Our guide to how wine is made places maceration in the full process.

Different compounds extract at different speeds.

  • Anthocyanins (colour) are water-soluble and come out early, in the first few days. Colour often peaks partway through fermentation, then drops slightly as some pigment binds with tannin or is lost.
  • Skin tannins come out steadily throughout fermentation, helped by rising alcohol and warmth.
  • Seed tannins are harsher and extract later, mainly once alcohol is high. Long, hot maceration on unripe seeds can make a wine bitter and astringent.

Our guide to sweetness, acidity and tannin in wine explains how tannin feels in the mouth.

Some winemakers hold crushed grapes cold, often around 5 to 10 °C, for a few days before fermentation starts. This is a cold soak or pre-fermentation maceration. The idea is to extract colour and fruit aromas in water before alcohol starts pulling out more tannin.

Cold soak needs refrigeration, careful sulphur dioxide use and clean fruit. Warm, damaged grapes can start fermenting with wild yeast or grow spoilage organisms during the hold. In India, where grapes can arrive at the winery warm, chilling the must quickly is often the first challenge.

As red wine ferments, carbon dioxide pushes the skins to the top, forming a thick layer called the cap. Left alone it dries out, extracts little and can grow acetic bacteria. Winemakers manage it in several ways:

  • Punch-down (pigeage). Pushing the cap down into the wine by hand or with a plunger. Gentle and good for delicate grapes such as Pinot Noir.
  • Pump-over (remontage). Drawing wine from the bottom of the tank and spraying it over the cap. Good for larger tanks and adds some oxygen to help yeast.
  • Rack and return (délestage). Draining the wine off the skins into another tank, then returning it over the cap in one go. Strong extraction and useful for removing some seeds.

A typical routine is two or three cap treatments a day during active fermentation, with more at the start and less as fermentation slows.

Red wines usually ferment warmer than whites, commonly around 25 to 30 °C. Warmth helps extraction. But fermentation produces heat. Above about 32 °C yeast becomes stressed and fermentation can stick. Fruit aromas can also be lost.

In India, this is the detail that decides most red fermentations. An open fermenter in a warm winery can climb several degrees in a day at peak activity. Without cooling jackets or a heat exchanger, a ferment that started at 26 °C can overheat by the third day. Check temperature in the cap and in the liquid at least twice a day, because the cap runs hotter than the liquid beneath it.

When fermentation finishes, the winemaker decides when to press. Pressing at dryness gives a fruit-forward wine. Some winemakers leave the wine on skins for days or weeks after fermentation, called extended or post-fermentation maceration. Over time tannins can feel softer and more integrated, though the reasons are still debated.

Taste the wine every day in the last part of maceration. When the tannin starts to feel drying rather than ripe, it is time to press. The press fraction matters too. Free-run wine drains naturally from the tank and is softer. Press wine squeezed from the skins is darker and more tannic. Many winemakers keep them separate and blend some press wine back in to taste.

Choosing maceration length, temperature and cap routine means tasting daily and knowing what each change will do. Getting it wrong cannot be fixed later.
faqs: How long should red wine macerate?
Usually through fermentation, around one to two weeks. Light styles may press earlier and structured wines may get extended maceration for days or weeks after.
Holding crushed red grapes cold before fermentation to extract colour and fruit aroma before alcohol pulls out more tannin.
Why do winemakers punch down the cap?
To keep the skins wet, extract colour and tannin evenly and stop the dry cap growing spoilage bacteria.
